outcomes: Judges whether a hole is usable (reachable and not challenged) or challenged (worth less)
Checks every enemy pawn and piece before relying on a hole
Picks the move that puts a piece on a usable hole

steps.text: A hole is a square your pawns can no longer guard (see the lesson *Holes: squares your pawns can no longer guard*). It helps the opponent only if a piece can **reach** it and **stay** there. So a hole gets one of two verdicts: **usable** (reachable and not challenged) or **challenged (worth less)** (a pawn or piece can challenge it, or no piece can get there).

Check three things. **Is it a hole?** None of the pawns of the side whose half of the board it lies in can ever guard it. **Can a piece reach it?** **Can an enemy pawn or piece attack that piece on the square?** As a *rule of thumb*, a hole is strong for one side only when its piece can land and stay; the same hole can be worth more in one position than in the next, so check it each time.

steps.title: Same hole, one knight moved
steps.prompt: Only the white knight has moved, from f3 to c3. Predict whether White can challenge the black knight on d5, then check.
Which part of the hole check did you find hardest to see: the pawns that can never guard it, the piece that can reach it, or the enemy piece that can challenge it?
